n:
*Study note:* *Psalm 131*. The psalmist affirms his humble dependence on the Lord and urges Israel to place its trust in God.

*Study note:* The precise significance of this title, which appears in {{Psalm 120|Pss 120-134}}, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 219-21.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my eyes are not lifted up.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I do not walk in great things, and in things too marvelous for me.”

*Translator's note:* Or “but.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I make level and make quiet my soul.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like a weaned [one] upon his mother.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like the weaned [one] upon me, my soul.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 132*. The psalmist reminds God of David’s devotion and of his promises concerning David’s dynasty and Zion.

*Study note:* The precise significance of this title, which appears in {{Psalm 120|Pss 120-134}}, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 219-21.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all his affliction.” This may refer to David’s strenuous and tireless efforts to make provision for the building of the temple (see 1 Chr 22:14). Some prefer to revocalize the text as עַנַוָתוֹ (ʿanavato, “his humility”).

*Translator's note:* The words “he said” are supplied in the translation to clarify that what follows is David’s vow.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the tent of my house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “go up upon the bed of my couch.”

*Translator's note:* The plural form of the noun may indicate degree or quality; David envisions a special dwelling place (see {{Psalm 43:3|Pss 43:3}}; {{Psalm 46:4|46:4}}; {{Psalm 84:1|84:1}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “the Mighty One of Jacob.”

*Translator's note:* Rather than having an antecedent, the third feminine singular pronominal suffix here (and in the next line) appears to refer to the ark of the covenant, mentioned in v. {{Psalm 132:8|8}}. (The Hebrew term אָרוֹן [ʾaron, “ark”] is sometimes construed as grammatically feminine. See {{1 Samuel 4:17|1 Sam 4:17}}; 2 Chr 8:11.)

*Study note:* Some understand *Ephrathah* as a reference to Kiriath Jearim because of the apparent allusion to this site in the next line (see the note on “Jaar”). The ark was kept in Kiriath Jearim after the Philistines released it (see {{1 Samuel 6:21|1 Sam 6:21-7:2}}). However, the switch in verbs from “heard about” to “found” suggests that Ephrathah not be equated with Jair. The group who is speaking heard about the ark while they were in Ephrath. They then went to retrieve it from Kiriath Jearim (“Jaar”). It is more likely that Ephrathah refers to a site near Bethel ({{Genesis 35:16|Gen 35:16}}, {{Genesis 35:19|19}}; {{Genesis 48:7|48:7}}) or to Bethlehem ({{Ruth 4:11|Ruth 4:11}}; {{Micah 5:2|Mic 5:2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fields of the forest.” The Hebrew term יָעַר (yaʿar, “forest”) is apparently a shortened alternative name for קִרְיַת יְעָרִים (qiryat yeʿarim, “Kiriath Jearim”), the place where the ark was kept after it was released by the Philistines and from which David and his men retrieved it (see 1 Chr 13:6).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not turn away the face of your anointed one.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord swore an oath to David [in] truth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he will not turn back from it.”

*Translator's note:* The words “he said” are supplied in the translation to clarify that what follows are the Lord’s words.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the fruit of your body.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he desired it for his dwelling place.”

*Translator's note:* The words “he said” are added in the translation to clarify that what follows are the Lord’s words.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for I desired it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will greatly bless her provision.” The infinitive absolute is used to emphasize the verb.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “her poor I will satisfy [with] food.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and her priests I will clothe [with] deliverance.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[with] shouting they will shout.” The infinitive absolute is used to emphasize the verb.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there I will cause a horn to sprout for David.” The horn of an ox underlies the metaphor (cf. {{Deuteronomy 33:17|Deut 33:17}}; {{1 Kings 22:11|1 Kgs 22:11}}; {{Psalm 18:2|Pss 18:2}}; {{Psalm 92:10|92:10}}). The horn of the wild ox is frequently a metaphor for military strength; the idiom “exalt the horn” signifies military victory (see {{1 Samuel 2:10|1 Sam 2:10}}; {{Psalm 89:17|Pss 89:17}}, {{Psalm 89:24|24}}; {{Psalm 92:10|92:10}}; Lam 2:17). In the ancient Near East powerful warrior-kings would sometimes compare themselves to a goring bull that used its horns to kill its enemies. For examples, see P. Miller, “El the Warrior,” *HTR* 60 (1967): 422-25, and R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 135-36.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I have arranged a lamp for my anointed one.” Here the “lamp” is a metaphor for the Davidic dynasty (see {{1 Kings 11:36|1 Kgs 11:36}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his enemies I will clothe [with] shame.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 133*. The psalmist affirms the benefits of family unity.

*Study note:* The precise significance of this title, which appears in {{Psalm 120|Pss 120-134}}, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 219-21.

*Study note:* This statement refers to the extended family structure of ancient Israel, where *brothers* would often live in proximity to one another ({{Deuteronomy 25:5|Deut 25:5}}), giving the family greater social prominence and security. However, in its later application in the nation of Israel it probably envisions unity within the covenant community. See L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 212-15.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[it is] like the good oil on the head, going down on the beard.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “which goes down in accordance with his measured things.” The Hebrew phrase מִדּוֹתָיו (middotayv, “his measured things”) refers here to the robes worn by Aaron. *HALOT* 546 s.v. *מַד derives the term from מַד (mad, “robe”) rather than מִדָּה (middah, “measured thing”). Ugaritic md means “robe” and is pluralized mdt.

*Study note:* *Hermon* refers to Mount Hermon, located north of Israel.

*Study note:* The *hills of Zion* are those surrounding Zion (see {{Psalm 87:1|Pss 87:1}}; {{Psalm 125:2|125:2}}). The psalmist does not intend to suggest that the dew from Mt. Hermon in the distant north actually flows down upon Zion. His point is that the same kind of heavy dew that replenishes Hermon may also be seen on Zion’s hills. See A. Cohen, *Psalms* (SoBB), 439. “Dew” here symbolizes divine blessing, as the next line suggests.

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there the Lord has commanded the blessing, life forever.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 134*. The psalmist calls on the temple servants to praise God (vv. 1-2). They in turn pronounce a blessing on the psalmist (v. 3).

*Study note:* The precise significance of this title, which appears in {{Psalm 120|Pss 120-134}}, is unclear. Perhaps worshipers recited these psalms when they ascended the road to Jerusalem to celebrate annual religious festivals. For a discussion of their background see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 219-21.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Look!”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stand.”

*Translator's note:* The pronominal suffix is second masculine singular, suggesting that the servants addressed in vv. {{Psalm 134:1|1-2}} are responding to the psalmist.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may the Lord bless you from Zion, the maker of heaven and earth.”
*Study note:* *Psalm 135*. The psalmist urges God’s people to praise him because he is the incomparable God and ruler of the world who has accomplished great things for Israel.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for [it is] pleasant.” The translation assumes that it is the Lord’s “name” that is pleasant. Another option is to understand the referent of “it” as the act of praising (see {{Psalm 147:1|Ps 147:1}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Study note:* *His special possession*. The language echoes {{Exodus 19:5|Exod 19:5}}; {{Deuteronomy 7:6|Deut 7:6}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:2|14:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:18|26:18}}. See also {{Malachi 3:17|Mal 3:17}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “signs” (see {{Psalm 65:8|Ps 65:8}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “portents”; “omens” (see {{Psalm 71:7|Ps 71:7}}). The Egyptian plagues are alluded to here.

*Translator's note:* Or “is forever.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O Lord, your remembrance [is] for a generation and a generation.” See {{Psalm 102:12|Ps 102:12}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “judges,” but here the idea is that the Lord “judges on behalf of” his people. The imperfect verbal forms here and in the next line draw attention to the Lord’s characteristic actions.

*Study note:* Verse {{Psalm 135:14|14}} echoes {{Deuteronomy 32:36|Deut 32:36}}, where Moses affirms that God mercifully relents from fully judging his wayward people.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the work of the hands of man.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “indeed, there is not breath in their mouth.” For the collocation אַף אֵין (ʾaf ʾen, “indeed, there is not”) see {{Isaiah 41:26|Isa 41:26}}. Another option is to take אַף as “nose” (see {{Psalm 115:6|Ps 115:6}}), in which case one might translate, “a nose, [but] they have no breath in their mouths.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will be.” Another option is to take the prefixed verbal form as a prayer, “may those who make them end up like them.”

*Study note:* Because the idols are lifeless, they cannot help their worshipers in times of crisis. Consequently the worshipers *end up* as dead as the gods in which they trust.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house” (here and in the next two lines).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “praised be the Lord from Zion.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 136*. In this hymn the psalmist affirms that God is praiseworthy because of his enduring loyal love, sovereign authority, and compassion. Each verse of the psalm concludes with the refrain “for his loyal love endures.”

*Translator's note:* Or “is forever.”

*Translator's note:* Or “cut.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Reed Sea” (also in v. {{Psalm 136:15|15}}). “Reed Sea” (or “Sea of Reeds”) is a more accurate rendering of the Hebrew expression יָם סוּף (yam suf), traditionally translated “Red Sea.” See the note on the term “Red Sea” in {{Exodus 13:18|Exod 13:18}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “into pieces.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who, in our low condition, remembered us.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to all flesh,” which can refer to all people (see {{Psalm 65:2|Pss 65:2}}; {{Psalm 145:21|145:21}}) or more broadly to mankind and animals. Elsewhere the psalms view God as the provider for all living things (see {{Psalm 104:27|Pss 104:27-28}}; {{Psalm 145:15|145:15}}).

*Study note:* *Psalm 137*. The Babylonian exiles lament their condition, vow to remain loyal to Jerusalem, and appeal to God for revenge on their enemies.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there we sit down, also we weep.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “ask us [for] the words of a song.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “our [?] joy.” The derivation and meaning of the Hebrew phrase תוֹלָלֵינוּ (tolalenu, “our [?]”) are uncertain. A derivation from תָּלַל (talal, “to mock”) fits contextually, but this root occurs only in the Hiphil stem. For a discussion of various proposals, see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 236.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from a song of Zion.” Most modern translations read, “one of the songs of Zion,” taking the preposition מִן (min, “from”) as partitive and “song” as collective. The present translation assumes the mem (ם) is enclitic, being misunderstood later as the prefixed preposition.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may my right hand forget.” In this case one must supply an object, such as “how to move” or “its skill.” The elliptical nature of the text has prompted emendations (see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* [WBC], 236). The translation assumes an emendation to תִּכְשַׁח (tikhshakh), from an otherwise unattested root כָּשַׁח (kashakh), meaning “to be crippled; to be lame.” See *HALOT* 502 s.v. כשׁח, which cites Arabic cognate evidence in support of the proposal. The difficulty of the MT can be explained as an error of transposition facilitated by the use of שָׁכַח (shakhakh, “forget”) just before this.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “if I do not lift up Jerusalem over the top of my joy.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “remember, O Lord, against the sons of Edom, the day of Jerusalem.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lay [it] bare, lay [it] bare.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O devastated daughter of Babylon.” The psalmist dramatically anticipates Babylon’s demise.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O the happiness of the one who repays you your wage which you paid to us.”

*Study note:* For other references to the wholesale slaughter of *babies* in the context of ancient Near Eastern warfare, see {{2 Kings 8:12|2 Kgs 8:12}}; {{Isaiah 13:16|Isa 13:16}}; Hos 13:16; Nah 3:10.

*Study note:* *Psalm 138*. The psalmist vows to thank the Lord for his deliverance and protection.

*Translator's note:* The referent of the Hebrew term אֱלֹהִים (ʾelohim) is unclear. It refers either to the angelic assembly (see {{Genesis 3:5|Gen 3:5}}; {{Psalm 8:5|Ps 8:5}}) or to the pagan gods (see {{Psalm 82:1|Pss 82:1}}, {{Psalm 82:6|6}}; {{Psalm 86:8|86:8}}; {{Psalm 97:7|97:7}}), in which case the psalmist’s praise takes on a polemical tone.

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads, “for you have made great over all your name your word.” If retained, this must mean that God’s mighty intervention, in fulfillment of his word of promise, surpassed anything he had done prior to this. However, the statement is odd and several emendations have been proposed. Some read, “for you have exalted over everything your name and your word,” while others suggest, “for you have exalted over all the heavens your name and your word.” The translation assumes an emendation of “your name” to “your heavens” (a construction that appears in {{Psalm 8:3|Pss 8:3}} and {{Psalm 144:5|144:5}}). The point is that God has been faithful to his promise and the reliability of that promise is apparent to all. For a fuller discussion of these options, see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 244.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the day.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you made me bold in my soul [with] strength.”

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal forms here and in the following verse are understood as jussives, for the psalmist appears to be calling upon the kings to praise God. Another option is to take them as imperfects and translate, “the kings of the earth will give thanks…and will sing.” In this case the psalmist anticipates a universal response to his thanksgiving song.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the words of your mouth.”

*Translator's note:* The Hifil of יָדַע II (yadaʿ) means “to humiliate,” causative of the Qal “be submissive, humbled, quiet” (cf. {{Job 21:19|Job 21:19}}; {{Proverbs 5:6|Prov 5:6}}; {{Isaiah 45:4|Isa 45:4}}; Jer 14:18; Hos 9:7). DCH supposes that the Qal can mean “to humiliate” in this verse. The more common homophonous root יָדַע means “to know,” sometimes with the nuance “to care for.” Alternatively the adjective גָּבֹהַּ (gavoah) can be understood as the subject, referring to God, “the exalted one cares for [the lowly] from a distance,” but the parallel thought in the next verse favors a contrast in this verse also.

*Text-critical note:* The form of the verb is יְיֵדָע (yeyedaʿ) commonly understood to be Qal of יָדַע I (yadaʿ), although the Qal should not have two yod’s. Most likely one י (yod) should be deleted as dittography, or the second should be read as a ו (vav) and the form be understood as a Hifil.

*Translator's note:* Or “distress.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “against the anger of my enemies you extend your hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “avenges on my behalf.” For the meaning “to avenge” for the verb גָּמַר (gamar), see *HALOT* 197-98 s.v. גמר.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the works of your hands.” Many medieval Hebrew mss read the singular, “work of your hands.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 139*. The psalmist acknowledges that God, who created him, is aware of his every action and thought. He invites God to examine his motives, for he is confident they are pure.

*Translator's note:* The statement is understood as generalizing—the psalmist describes what God typically does.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my traveling and my lying down you measure.” The verb זָרָה (zarah, “to measure”) is probably here a denominative from זֶרֶת (zeret, “a span; a measure”), though some derive it from זָרָה (zarat, “to winnow; to sift”; see BDB 279-80 s.v. זָרָה).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all my ways.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “look, O Lord, you know all of it.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “too amazing [is this] knowledge for me, it is elevated, I cannot attain to it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Where can I go from your spirit, and where from your face can I flee?” God’s “spirit” may refer here (1) to his presence (note the parallel term, “your face,” and see {{Psalm 104:29|Ps 104:29-30}}, where God’s “face” is his presence and his “spirit” is the life-giving breath he imparts) or (2) to his personal Spirit (see {{Psalm 51:10|Ps 51:10}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb סָלַק (salaq, “to ascend”) occurs only here in the OT, but the word is well-attested in Aramaic literature from different time periods and displays a wide semantic range (see *DNWSI* 2:788-90).

*Translator's note:* The verb יָצַע (yatzaʿ) is rare in the Bible (see {{Isaiah 58:5|Isa 58:5}} also Hiphil, and {{Isaiah 1:14|Isa 1:14}}; Est 4:3 for Hophal examples). There are three main options for understanding this phrase. It may mean “to descend to Sheol,” as in the LXX. This takes the motion in the verb as very generic for this context and understands “Sheol” without a preposition as the default “to Sheol.” Many translations take it as spreading out [something] to act as a bed, couch, or area to lie down. It is uncertain that the idea of a bed has to be implied and this does not required to fit the other contexts. Or, as taken here, it may “to spread [oneself] out, to sprawl.” Each view has merits and it is difficult to decide because the are so few examples.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “look, you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “rise up.”

*Study note:* *On the wings of the dawn*. This personification of the “dawn” may find its roots in mythological traditions about the god Shachar, whose birth is described in an Ugaritic myth (see G. R. Driver, *Canaanite Myths and Legends*, 126) and who is mentioned in {{Isaiah 14:12|Isa 14:12}} as the father of Helel.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at the end.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb שׁוּף (shuf), which means “to crush; to wound,” in {{Genesis 3:15|Gen 3:15}} and {{Job 9:17|Job 9:17}}, is problematic here. For a discussion of attempts to relate the verb to Arabic roots, see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 251. Many emend the form to יְשׂוּכֵּנִי (yesukkeni), from the root שָׂכַך (sakhakh, “to cover,” an alternate form of סָכַך [sakhakh]), a reading assumed in the present translation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and night, light, around me.”

*Translator's note:* The words “to see” are supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “shines like.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like darkness, like light.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my kidneys.” The kidneys were sometimes viewed as the seat of one’s emotions and moral character (cf. {{Psalm 7:9|Pss 7:9}}; {{Psalm 26:2|26:2}}). A number of translations, recognizing that “kidneys” does not communicate this idea to the modern reader, have generalized the concept: “inmost being” (NAB, NIV); “inward parts” (NASB, NRSV); “the delicate, inner parts of my body” (NLT). In the last instance, the focus is almost entirely on the physical body rather than the emotions or moral character. The present translation, by using a hendiadys (one concept expressed through two terms), links the concepts of emotion (heart) and moral character (mind).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb סָכַךְ (sakhakh, “to weave together”) is an alternate form of שָׂכַךְ (sakhakh, “to weave”) used in {{Job 10:11|Job 10:11}}.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “because awesome things, I am distinct, amazing [are] your works.” The text as it stands is syntactically problematic and makes little, if any, sense. The Niphal of פָּלָה (palah) occurs elsewhere only in {{Exodus 33:16|Exod 33:16}}. Many take the form from פָלָא (palaʾ; see GKC 216 §75.*qq*), which in the Niphal perfect means “to be amazing” (see {{2 Samuel 1:26|2 Sam 1:26}}; {{Psalm 118:23|Ps 118:23}}; {{Proverbs 30:18|Prov 30:18}}). Some, following the LXX and some other ancient witnesses, also prefer to emend the verb from first to second person, “you are amazing” (see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* [WBC], 249, 251). The present translation assumes the text conflates two variants: נִפְלָאִים (niflaʾim), the otherwise unattested masculine plural participle of פָלָא, and נִפְלָאוֹת (niflaʾot), the usual (feminine) plural form of the Niphal participle. The latter has been changed to a verb by later scribes in an attempt to accommodate it syntactically. The original text likely read, נוראות נפלאותים מעשׂיך (“your works [are] awesome [and] amazing”).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “and my being knows very much.” Better parallelism is achieved (see v. {{Psalm 139:15|15a}}) if one emends יֹדַעַת (yodaʿat), a Qal active participle, feminine singular form, to יָדַעְתָּ (yadaʿta), a Qal perfect second masculine singular perfect. See L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 252.

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew term אֲשֶׁר (ʾasher, “which”) should probably be emended to כֲּאַשֶׁר (kaʾasher, “when”). The כ (kaf) may have been lost by haplography (note the kaf at the end of the preceding form).

*Study note:* The phrase *depths of the earth* may be metaphorical (euphemistic) or it may reflect a prescientific belief about the origins of the embryo deep beneath the earth’s surface (see H. W. Wolff, *Anthropology of the Old Testament*, 96-97). {{Job 1:21|Job 1:21}} also closely associates the mother’s womb with the earth.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Your eyes saw my shapeless form.” The Hebrew noun גֹּלֶם (golem) occurs only here in the OT. In later Hebrew the word refers to “a lump, a shapeless or lifeless substance,” and to “unfinished matter, a vessel wanting finishing” (Jastrow 222 s.v. גּוֹלֶם). The translation employs the dynamic rendering “when I was inside the womb” to clarify that the speaker was still in his mother’s womb at the time he was “seen” by God.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and on your scroll all of them were written, [the] days [which] were formed, and [there was] not one among them.” This “scroll” may be the “scroll of life” mentioned in {{Psalm 69:28|Ps 69:28}} (see the note on the word “living” there).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and to me how precious are your thoughts, O God.” The Hebrew verb יָקַר (yaqar) probably has the sense of “difficult [to comprehend]” here (see *HALOT* 432 s.v. יקר qal.1 and note the use of Aramaic יַקִּר in Dan 2:11). Elsewhere in the immediate context the psalmist expresses his amazement at the extent of God’s knowledge about him (see vv. {{Psalm 139:1|1-6}}, {{Psalm 139:17|17b-18}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “how vast are their heads.” Here the Hebrew word “head” is used of the “sum total” of God’s knowledge of the psalmist.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “I awake and I [am] still with you.” A reference to the psalmist awaking from sleep makes little, if any, sense contextually. For this reason some propose an emendation to הֲקִצּוֹתִי (haqitsoti), a Hiphil perfect form from an otherwise unattested verb קָצַץ (qatsats) understood as a denominative of קֵץ (qets, “end”). See L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 252-53.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew particle אִם (ʾim, “if”) and following prefixed verbal form here express a wish (see {{Psalm 81:8|Pss 81:8}}; {{Psalm 95:7|95:7}}, as well as GKC 321 §109.*b*).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “men of bloodshed.”

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “they speak [of] you.” The suffixed form of the verb אָמַר (ʾamar, “to speak”) is peculiar. The translation assumes an emendation to יַמְרֻךָ (yamrukha), a Hiphil form from מָרָה (marah, “to rebel”; see {{Psalm 78:40|Ps 78:40}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by deceit.”

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “lifted up for emptiness, your cities.” The form נָשֻׂא (nasuʾ; a Qal passive participle) should be emended to נָשְׂאוּ (naseʾu; a Qal perfect, third common plural, “[they] lift up”). Many emend עָרֶיךָ (ʿarekha, “your cities”) to עָלֶיךָ (ʿalekha, “against you”), but it is preferable to understand the noun as an Aramaism and translate “your enemies” (see Dan 4:16 and L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* [WBC], 253).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “who raise themselves up against you.” The form וּבִתְקוֹמְמֶיךָ (uvitqomemekha) should be emended to וּבְמִתְקוֹמְמֶיךָ (uvemitqomemekha), a Hitpolel participle (the prefixed מ [mem] of the participle is accidentally omitted in the MT, though a few medieval Hebrew mss have it).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[with] completeness of hatred I hate them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and know my heart.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun שַׂרְעַפַּי (sarʿappay, “concerns”) is used of “worries” in {{Psalm 94:19|Ps 94:19}}.

*Translator's note:* Many understand the Hebrew term עֹצֶב (ʿotsev) as a noun meaning “pain,” and translate the phrase דֶּרֶךְ עֹצֶב (derekh ʿotsev) as “of pain,” but this makes little sense here. (Some interpret it to refer to actions which bring pain to others.) It is preferable to take עֹצֶב as “idol” (see *HALOT* 865 s.v. I עֹצֶב) and understand “way of an idol” to refer to idolatrous actions or tendency. See L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 253.

*Translator's note:* *Or* “in the ancient path.” This phrase may refer to the moral path prescribed by the Lord at the beginning of Israel’s history. See Jer 6:16; 18:15, as well as L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 253.

*Study note:* *Psalm 140*. The psalmist asks God to deliver him from his deadly enemies, calls judgment down upon them, and affirms his confidence in God’s justice.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from a wicked man.” The Hebrew uses the singular in a representative or collective sense (note the plural verbs in v. {{Psalm 140:2|2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a man of violent acts.” The Hebrew uses the singular in a representative or collective sense (note the plural verbs in v. {{Psalm 140:2|2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they devise wicked [plans] in [their] mind.”

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “they attack [for] war.” Some revocalize the verb (which is a Qal imperfect from גּוּר, gur, “to attack”) as יְגָרוּ (yegaru), a Piel imperfect from גָרָה (garah, “stir up strife”). This is followed in the present translation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they sharpen their tongue like a serpent.” {{Psalm 64:3|Ps 64:3}} reads, “they sharpen their tongues like sword.” Perhaps {{Psalm 140:3|Ps 140:3}} uses a mixed metaphor, the point being that “they sharpen their tongues [like a sword],” as it were, so that when they speak, their words wound like a serpent’s bite. Another option is that the language refers to the pointed or forked nature of a serpent’s tongue, which is viewed metaphorically as “sharpened.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term is used only here in the OT.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “under.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to push down my steps.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and ropes,” but many prefer to revocalize the noun as a participle (חֹבְלִים, khovelim) from the verb חָבַל (khaval, “act corruptly”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the strength of my deliverance.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “cover.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his.” The singular is used in a representative sense (see v. {{Psalm 140:1|1}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his plot do not promote, they rise up.” The translation understands the final verb as being an unmarked temporal clause. Another option is to revocalize the verb as a Hiphil and take the verb with the next verse, “those who surround me lift up [their] head,” which could refer to their proud attitude as they anticipate victory (see {{Psalm 27:6|Ps 27:6}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “harm of their lips.” The genitive here indicates the source or agent of the harm.

*Translator's note:* The verb form in the *Kethib* (consonantal Hebrew text) appears to be a Hiphil imperfect from the root מוּט (mut, “to sway”), but the Hiphil occurs only here and in {{Psalm 55:3|Ps 55:3}}, where it is preferable to read יַמְטִירוּ (yamtiru, “they rain down”). In {{Psalm 140:10|Ps 140:10}} the form יַמְטֵר (yamter, “let him rain down”) should probably be read.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “into bottomless pits, they will not arise.” The translation assumes that the preposition ב (bet) has the nuance “from” here. Another option is to connect the line with what precedes, take the final clause as an asyndetic relative clause, and translate, “into bottomless pits [from which] they cannot arise.” The Hebrew noun מַהֲמֹרָה (mahamorah, “bottomless pit”) occurs only here in the OT.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a man of a tongue.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for blows.” The Hebrew noun מַדְחֵפֹה (madkhefoh, “blow”) occurs only here in the OT.

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows the *Qere* and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading a first person verb form here. The *Kethib* reads the second person.
